A = ["vol_20d"]

# Some things are easier to predict than others

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11.0, 3.4), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(R.index, R.values, color=BLUE, linewidth=0.9)
axes[0].axhline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=0.9)
axes[0].set_ylabel("daily return (%)")
axes[0].set_title("Apple, every trading day", loc="left")
v = R.rolling(20).std()
axes[1].plot(v.index, v.values, color=BRICK, linewidth=1.8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("volatility (%)")
axes[1].set_title("The same days, as a 20-day standard deviation", loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Returns are close to unpredictable. Volatility is not. **It clusters**: calm
months are followed by calm months, so today's volatility says something about
next month's.


# Today

- fit a model with **scikit-learn** and score it on unseen days
- compare it with two rules that need no model at all
- see why the lowest error is often the wrong model to keep
- hold out a **validation** block, and see why one is not enough
- use **cross-validation**, with folds that respect the calendar

<br>

The lecture introduces each of these. The exercises and the case are where you
practise them.


# 1 · Fitting a model {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 1
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Setting up the prediction problem, and fitting a linear regression to it.
:::


# The question

**How volatile will Apple be over the next twenty trading days?**

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Why it matters** <span>option prices, margin requirements and risk limits are all set from a volatility forecast</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**What you know today** <span>how volatile the last twenty days were, how volatile the last sixty were, and how the stock has drifted</span>
:::
:::

::: {.muted .small}
The answer is not known for twenty days, which makes this a forecast rather
than a description.
:::


# The table

```{pyodide}
prices = pd.read_csv("data/prices.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
rets = prices.pivot(index="date", columns="ticker", values="close").pct_change().dropna() * 100

r = rets["AAPL"]

table = pd.DataFrame({
    "vol_20d": r.rolling(20).std(),
    "vol_60d": r.rolling(60).std(),
    "ret_20d": r.rolling(20).mean(),
})
table["vol_next"] = r.rolling(20).std().shift(-20)
table = table.dropna()

table.head(3)
```

::: {.muted .small}
`rolling` and `shift` were both covered last time. Multiplying by 100 converts
the returns to percent, which keeps the numbers easier to read.
:::


# The three features and the target

table.shape

# Is there anything there?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 3.0))
ax.scatter(TBL["vol_20d"], TBL["vol_next"], s=8, color=BLUE, alpha=0.30,
           linewidths=0)
ax.set_xlabel("volatility of the last 20 days (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("volatility of the next 20 days (%)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each dot is one day. The cloud slopes upwards, so a volatile month tends to be
followed by another one. A linear regression finds the line through it.


# Splitting by date

```{pyodide}
train = table.loc[:"2022-12-31"]
test = table.loc["2023-01-01":]

print(len(train))
print(len(test))
```

::: {.keypoint}
Split on a **date**, not at random. A random test day would sit between two
training days with almost identical volatility, so the score would come out too
good.
:::


# X and y

scikit-learn takes the features and the target as two separate objects.

```{pyodide}
X_train = train[["vol_20d"]]
y_train = train["vol_next"]

X_train.head(3)
```

::: {.muted .small}
Two pairs of brackets: the inner pair is a **list of columns**, as in
`prices[["date", "close"]]`. One pair returns a single column, which cannot be
used as `X`.
:::


# scikit-learn

scikit-learn contains all sorts of models, and it is already installed in
Colab.

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Models** <span>linear regression today; ridge, lasso and trees later in the course</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Metrics** <span>mean squared error, R², and the other scoring measures covered last time</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Splitting** <span>tools for dividing the data into training, validation and test blocks</span>
:::
:::

::: {.muted .small}
The package is installed under the name `scikit-learn` but imported as
`sklearn`.
:::


# Import, create, fit

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(model)
```

`LinearRegression()` creates a model that has not been fitted to anything yet.
Calling `.fit()` with the training features and the training target computes the
coefficients.

::: {.muted .small}
Printing the model shows only which kind of model it is. The coefficients it
computed are stored on the object itself.
:::


# What it learned

```{pyodide}
print(model.intercept_)
print(model.coef_)
```

::: {.muted .small}
A trailing underscore marks an attribute **computed from the data**.
`model.coef_` does not exist until `.fit()` has run.
:::


# Reading the two numbers

::: {.formula}
$$
\widehat{\text{vol}}_{\text{next}} = 0.88 + 0.49 \times \text{vol}_{20d}
$$
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression as _LR
_m = _LR().fit(TRAIN[A], TRAIN["vol_next"])
gx = np.linspace(TBL["vol_20d"].min(), TBL["vol_20d"].max(), 50)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.4, 2.6))
ax.scatter(TBL["vol_20d"], TBL["vol_next"], s=8, color=GREY_LIGHT, alpha=0.6,
           linewidths=0)
ax.plot(gx, _m.intercept_ + _m.coef_[0] * gx, color=BLUE, linewidth=2.4)
ax.set_xlabel("volatility of the last 20 days (%)")
ax.set_ylabel("volatility of the next 20 days (%)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The slope is 0.49, not 1: only half of this month's excess volatility carries
into next month. **Volatility is pulled back towards its average**, which is
called mean reversion.


# Predicting

```{pyodide}
X_test = test[["vol_20d"]]

predictions = model.predict(X_test)
predictions[:5]
```

::: {.muted .small}
`.predict()` returns one number per row of `X_test`. These are days in 2023 and
2024, none of which were used to fit the model.
:::


# The forecast, against what happened

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
_pred = _m.predict(TEST[A])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11.0, 2.8))
ax.plot(TEST.index, TEST["vol_next"], color=AMBER, linewidth=1.6,
        label="what happened")
ax.plot(TEST.index, _pred, color=BLUE, linewidth=1.6, label="the forecast")
ax.set_ylabel("20-day volatility (%)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The forecast tracks the broad moves but lags at every turn. Comparing it with
anything else needs a number, not a picture.


# 2 · Scoring the model {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 2
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Measuring the error, and choosing something sensible to compare it with.
:::


# Mean squared error

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], predictions)
```

::: {.muted .small}
Every metric in scikit-learn takes the true values first and the predictions
second.
:::


# Root mean squared error

```{pyodide}
rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], predictions))
print(rmse)
```

The square root puts the error back into percentage points: **the forecast is
wrong by about 0.41 percentage points on a typical day.**


# Is 0.41 good?

An RMSE of 0.41 does not mean anything on its own. To judge it, compare it
against two rules that are so simple they need no model.

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Guess the average** <span>predict the same number every day and ignore the features entirely</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Repeat what just happened** <span>predict that the next twenty days will be as volatile as the last twenty</span>
:::
:::

::: {.muted .small}
Neither rule has parameters and neither needs fitting. Together they set the
minimum that a model has to beat.
:::


# Rule one: always guess the average

```{pyodide}
guess = train["vol_next"].mean()
print(guess)

flat = [guess] * len(test)
print(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], flat)))
```

::: {.muted .small}
The average is computed on the **training** rows. Using the test average would
require information that was not available when the forecast was made.
:::


# Rule two: repeat this month

```{pyodide}
print(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], test["vol_20d"])))
```

The forecast for the next twenty days is simply the last twenty, with no
fitting involved. Because volatility clusters, it is already accurate.


# The three forecasts compared

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error as _mse
_base = TRAIN["vol_next"].mean()
_vals = [float(np.sqrt(_mse(TEST["vol_next"], np.full(len(TEST), _base)))),
         float(np.sqrt(_mse(TEST["vol_next"], TEST["vol_20d"]))),
         float(np.sqrt(_mse(TEST["vol_next"], _m.predict(TEST[A]))))]
_names = ["guess the\naverage", "repeat this\nmonth", "the fitted\nmodel"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 2.6))
bars = ax.bar(_names, _vals, color=[GREY, BLUE_LIGHT, BLUE], width=0.5)
for b, vv in zip(bars, _vals):
    ax.text(b.get_x() + b.get_width() / 2, vv + 0.012, "%.3f" % vv,
            ha="center", fontsize=12, color="#52514e")
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.62)
ax.set_ylabel("test RMSE (percentage points)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The model wins, but only by about three percent over a rule with no parameters.
**Margins that small are normal in finance.**

Fit the same model on `vol_60d` instead of `vol_20d`, and score it the same
way. Does the longer window predict better?

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
long_model = LinearRegression()
long_model.fit(...)

long_pred = long_model.predict(test[["vol_60d"]])
print(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], long_pred)))
```

::: {.muted .small}
`.fit()` takes two arguments, and the last two lines show what shape each
one has.
:::


# Your turn 1: answer

```python
long_model.fit(train[["vol_60d"]], train["vol_next"])
```

**0.419**, against 0.406 for `vol_20d`. A sixty-day average reacts more slowly,
so it lags further at the turns.

::: {.muted .small}
The features come from `train`, not `test`, and need the same double brackets
as `predict`. The target is one column, so it takes a single pair.
:::

::: {.muted .small}
A natural next question is whether using both features together does better
than either one alone.
:::


# 3 · Choosing between models {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 3
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Comparing several models, and deciding which one to keep.
:::


# Three candidates

```{pyodide}
A = ["vol_20d"]
B = ["vol_20d", "vol_60d"]
C = ["vol_20d", "vol_60d", "ret_20d"]
```

All three use the same model, the same rows and the same target. They differ
only in which columns go into `X`.

::: {.muted .small}
Naming the three lists here lets the later slides write `train[A]` instead of
repeating the column names.
:::


# Scoring on the training rows

```{pyodide}
for columns in [A, B, C]:
    m = LinearRegression()
    m.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])
    error = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(train["vol_next"], m.predict(train[columns])))
    print(len(columns), "features:", round(error, 4))
```

The error falls each time a column is added.


# More columns always fit better

Adding a column can never worsen the fit. A useless column can be given a
coefficient of zero, reproducing the previous fit exactly.

::: {.keypoint}
Training error therefore always favours the largest model. It measures the fit
on these rows, not whether the extra columns help on new ones.
:::

::: {.muted .small}
This is overfitting: a model with enough freedom fits the noise in its own
training rows.
:::


# Scoring on the test rows

```{pyodide}
for columns in [A, B, C]:
    m = LinearRegression()
    m.fit(train[columns], train["vol_next"])
    error = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], m.predict(test[columns])))
    print(len(columns), "features:", round(error, 4))
```

The ranking reverses. **The one-feature model has the lowest test error**, so
the two extra columns were fitting noise rather than signal.


# So use the test rows to choose?

It is tempting. The test rows are the honest out-of-sample score, and they just
gave a clear answer.

::: {.keypoint}
The problem is what the word **lowest** is doing. Three test errors were
computed and the smallest was kept. Part of being smallest is being genuinely
better, and part of it is luck.
:::

::: {.muted .small}
The winner's 0.406 is therefore too good. It is the best of three draws, not an
unbiased estimate of what the model will do next year.
:::


# It gets worse with every choice

Three candidates is mild. A real project compares far more, and every
comparison is another look at the test rows.

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Features** <span>which columns to include, which to transform, how long a window to use</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Settings** <span>every model from here has them: ridge has a shrinkage parameter, a tree has a depth</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**And they multiply** <span>ten settings tried on four feature sets is forty looks at the test rows</span>
:::
:::

::: {.keypoint}
Nothing from the test rows ever entered the code. It entered through **your
decisions**, which is the hardest kind of leakage to notice.
:::


# Choosing and reporting are different jobs

<div class="compare">
<div class="compare-col">
<h3>Choosing</h3>
<p>Comparing candidates and keeping one. This happens repeatedly, and every comparison uses up a little of the honesty of whatever rows it was done on.</p>
</div>
<div class="compare-col cmp-alt">
<h3>Reporting</h3>
<p>Measuring how well the chosen model does on rows that played no part in the choosing. This happens once, and that number is the one reported.</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.keypoint}
Two jobs means two blocks of data. Choosing needs held-out rows of its own.
:::


# A third block, for choosing

# Cutting the training block in two

# Choosing on the validation block

```{pyodide}
for columns in [A, B, C]:
    m = LinearRegression()
    m.fit(fit[columns], fit["vol_next"])
    error = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(val["vol_next"], m.predict(val[columns])))
    print(len(columns), "features:", round(error, 4))
```

The **three-feature model wins**, and the test rows played no part in it. On
the test rows the ranking was the other way round.

# 4 · One split is one experiment {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 4
:::

::: {.divider-note}
What happens when the validation block is placed somewhere else.
:::


# Two cuts, two winners

2021 and 2022 were chosen for convenience, not for any real reason. Moving the
cut changed which model came out best.

::: {.keypoint}
When the cut date determines which model is kept, the result says more about
the choice of cut date than about the models.
:::


# Every cut date, side by side

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression as _LR2
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error as _mse2

_cuts = ["2018-12-31", "2019-12-31", "2020-12-31", "2021-12-31"]
_sets = [A, B, C]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11.0, 2.6))
for ax, cut in zip(axes, _cuts):
    f = TRAIN.loc[:cut]
    v = TRAIN.loc[cut:]
    errs = []
    for cols in _sets:
        mm = _LR2().fit(f[cols], f["vol_next"])
        errs.append(float(np.sqrt(_mse2(v["vol_next"], mm.predict(v[cols])))))
    best = int(np.argmin(errs))
    lo, hi = min(errs), max(errs)
    pad = (hi - lo) * 0.55 + 1e-9
    for i, e in enumerate(errs):
        on = i == best
        ax.plot([i, i], [lo - pad, e], color=GREY_LIGHT, linewidth=1.2,
                zorder=1)
        ax.scatter([i], [e], s=140 if on else 70,
                   color=BLUE if on else GREY, zorder=3)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 2.6)
    ax.set_ylim(lo - pad, hi + pad)
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1, 2])
    ax.set_xticklabels(["1", "2", "3"])
    ax.set_title("cut at end of " + cut[:4], loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("features")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=9.5)
    ax.text(best, hi + pad * 0.55, "best", ha="center", fontsize=10.5,
            color=BLUE, fontweight="600")
axes[0].set_ylabel("validation RMSE")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

With the cut after 2018 or 2019 the one-feature model has the lowest error.
With the cut after 2020 or 2021 the three-feature model does.

::: {.muted .small}
Each panel has its own scale, so compare the dots within a panel, not across
them.
:::


# Why the winner changes

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Each block is a single period** <span>2020 contains a crash and 2021 does not, so the two periods favour different models</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Each block is small** <span>a few hundred rows, and consecutive rows overlap heavily because their windows do</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Validation rows are not fitted on** <span>every row held back for validation is a row the model does not learn from</span>
:::
:::

::: {.keypoint}
The candidates differ by less than the periods do, so one cut date cannot
separate them.
:::


# Using several cut dates

Since the cut dates disagree, there is no reason to trust any one of them.
**Use several cut dates and average the results.**

::: {.muted .small}
Every cut is an honest measurement on its own. Averaging them stops any single
period deciding the winner.
:::


# 5 · Cross-validation {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 5
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Averaging over several cut dates, and reading the result.
:::


# Every row takes a turn

Split the training rows into $K$ blocks, called **folds**. Each fold is held
back once, scored by a model fitted without it, and the $K$ scores are averaged.

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**$K$ measurements, not one** <span>the average of five is far steadier than any one of them, as the four cut dates already showed</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Every row is scored once** <span>no row is left out of the judging, so no part of the sample is ignored</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**And still fitted on** <span>each row is used for fitting in the other folds, so none is permanently lost to validation</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**The spread comes free** <span>$K$ numbers say how much the answer moves from period to period, which one number cannot</span>
:::
:::


# The arithmetic

Write $\mathcal{F}_k$ for the rows scored in fold $k$, and $n_k$ for how many
there are:

::: {.formula}
$$
e_k = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_k}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{F}_k}\left(y_i - \hat{y}_i\right)^2}
\qquad\qquad
\text{CV}_K = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} e_k
$$
:::

- every $\hat{y}_i$ comes from a model fitted **without** fold $k$
- $e_k$ is the RMSE on one fold, and $\text{CV}_K$ is the average of the $K$ of them
- drop the square root and $\text{CV}_K$ is the textbook version, in MSE


# Five cuts instead of one

::: {.muted .small}
The scored block always comes after the fitted rows. Each cut is a **fold**,
and averaging over folds is **cross-validation**.
:::


# TimeSeriesSplit

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

folds = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

for fit_rows, score_rows in folds.split(train):
    print(len(fit_rows), "fitted", len(score_rows), "scored")
```

::: {.muted .small}
`.split()` returns the row positions for each fold. `cross_val_score` runs this
loop automatically, but printing it once shows what the folds actually
contain.
:::


# cross_val_score

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), train[A], train["vol_next"],
                         cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
scores
```

The call fits five models and returns five scores. Each fold is scored by a
model that was not fitted on it.


# Why they are negative

scikit-learn reports every score so that **larger is better**. Errors are
flipped to negative to fit that convention.

```{pyodide}
print(-scores)
print(-scores.mean())
```

::: {.muted .small}
A value of `-0.583` means an RMSE of `0.583`. Remove the minus sign before
reporting it.
:::


# The five fold scores

<div class="statband">
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.583</span><div class="stat-label">2016-17</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.703</span><div class="stat-label">2017-19</div></div>
<div class="stat stat-warn"><span class="stat-big">1.255</span><div class="stat-label">2019-20</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.582</span><div class="stat-label">2020-21</div></div>
<div class="stat"><span class="stat-big">0.580</span><div class="stat-label">2021-22</div></div>
</div>

Four of the folds give similar errors and one is roughly twice as large. That
fold is scored on the period containing **March 2020**.

::: {.keypoint}
Two models can share an average and differ completely: one steady across five
folds, another poor in one. Report the spread as well.
:::


# Choosing with cross-validation

```{pyodide}
for columns in [A, B, C]:
    scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), train[columns], train["vol_next"],
                             cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    print(len(columns), "features:", round(-scores.mean(), 4))
```

The **one-feature model has the lowest average error**. That result is an
average over five cut dates rather than a single measurement.

# 6 · KFold and time order {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 6
:::

::: {.divider-note}
The standard form of cross-validation, and why it does not suit this table.
:::


# When the rows are not in time order

`KFold` shuffles the rows and cuts the folds anywhere, which assumes the rows
are interchangeable. That holds for a table of loan applications, or of firms.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
n_demo = 120
rs = np.random.default_rng(4)
fold_shuf = rs.integers(0, 5, n_demo)
fold_block = np.minimum(np.arange(n_demo) // 24, 4)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(11.0, 2.3), sharex=True)
pal = [BLUE, BLUE_LIGHT, GREY, AMBER, BRICK]
for ax, flags, ttl in [
    (axes[0], fold_shuf, "KFold: the folds are shuffled through the rows"),
    (axes[1], fold_block, "TimeSeriesSplit: the folds move forward in time"),
]:
    ax.bar(np.arange(n_demo), np.ones(n_demo), width=1.0,
           color=[pal[f] for f in flags])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=12)
    for side in ("left", "bottom"):
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
axes[1].set_xlabel("row")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


# KFold on the three candidates

```{pyodide}
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

shuffled = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

for columns in [A, B, C]:
    scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), train[columns], train["vol_next"],
                             cv=shuffled, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    print(len(columns), "features:", round(-scores.mean(), 4))
```

`KFold` gives the lowest error to the three-feature model, which had the
**highest** error on the test rows.


# Why shuffled folds flatter the score

# The same overlap, at the boundary

The last rows in a fitting block have targets that extend twenty days into the
block used for scoring. The `gap` argument drops those rows.

```{pyodide}
gapped = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5, gap=20)

scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), train[A], train["vol_next"],
                         cv=gapped, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(round(-scores.mean(), 4))
```

::: {.muted .small}
The change is small because twenty rows are little against blocks of several
hundred. It matters far more when the target spans a longer window.
:::


# Expanding and rolling windows

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit as _TSS

n_row = 600
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.0, 2.7), sharey=True)
for ax, cvo, ttl in [
    (axes[0], _TSS(n_splits=5), "expanding: keep every past row"),
    (axes[1], _TSS(n_splits=5, max_train_size=120), "rolling: keep the last two years"),
]:
    for i, (tr, va) in enumerate(cvo.split(np.arange(n_row))):
        ax.barh(5 - i, len(tr), left=tr[0], height=0.55, color=BLUE)
        ax.barh(5 - i, len(va), left=va[0], height=0.55, color=AMBER)
        if i == 0:
            ax.text(len(tr) / 2, 5.55, "fit", ha="center", fontsize=10.5,
                    color=BLUE, fontweight="600")
            ax.text(va[0] + len(va) / 2, 5.55, "score", ha="center",
                    fontsize=10.5, color="#8a6508", fontweight="600")
    ax.set_xlim(0, n_row)
    ax.set_ylim(0.4, 6.0)
    ax.set_yticks(range(1, 6))
    ax.set_yticklabels(["cut 5", "cut 4", "cut 3", "cut 2", "cut 1"], fontsize=10)
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_xlabel("trading day")
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=12.5)
    ax.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(left=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`max_train_size=500` produces the version on the right. Use a rolling window
when older years have stopped being relevant, and an expanding window when they
have not.


# 7 · More candidates than three {.divider}

::: {.divider-kicker}
Part 7
:::

::: {.divider-note}
Searching a long list of feature sets, and knowing when to stop.
:::


# Where the candidates come from

These three feature sets were written by hand. With $p$ features there are
$2^p$ subsets: a thousand at ten features, a million at twenty.

::: {.keypoint}
Fitting every subset stops being possible at about twenty features. The usual
answer is to walk through the subsets one feature at a time instead.
:::


# Three ways to walk

::: {.why-grid}
::: {.why-point}
**Forward selection** <span>start with nothing. Add the feature that lowers the error most, then the best of those left, and stop when it stops falling.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Backward selection** <span>start with every feature. Drop the one that costs least, and repeat. It needs more rows than features to get started.</span>
:::
::: {.why-point}
**Stepwise selection** <span>forward, but after each addition check whether an earlier feature has become redundant and can be dropped.</span>
:::
:::

::: {.muted .small}
At ten features, forward selection fits 55 models instead of 1,024. None of the
three is guaranteed to find the best subset, and all three usually get close.
:::


# AIC and BIC

Each walk still needs a rule for when to stop. AIC and BIC score a model by its
fit **and** its size, so the two can be traded off in one number:

::: {.formula}
$$
\text{AIC} = n\log(\text{MSE}) + 2d
\qquad\qquad
\text{BIC} = n\log(\text{MSE}) + d\log(n)
$$
:::

- the first term falls as the fit improves, the second charges for each of the $d$ parameters
- smaller is better, and adding a useless feature raises the total
- $\log(n)$ is larger than 2 here, so BIC charges more and prefers smaller models

::: {.muted .small}
One fit per candidate and no folds at all, which is why they are still used.
Cross-validation is slower but assumes nothing about the shape of the errors.
:::


# The order it all happens in

::: {.diagram}
<svg width="1000" height="235" viewBox="0 0 1000 235" role="img" aria-label="The workflow: seal the test rows, list candidates, cross-validate on the training rows, choose, refit on all training rows, then score once on the test rows">
  <rect x="8" y="38" width="148" height="66" rx="8" fill="#fbf1f0" stroke="#b3402f" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="82" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" fill="#b3402f" font-weight="600">1. seal the</text>
  <text x="82" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" fill="#b3402f" font-weight="600">test rows</text>
  <rect x="176" y="38" width="148" height="66" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#86b6ef" stroke-width="1.6"/>
  <text x="250" y="66" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" fill="#0d366b" font-weight="600">2. list the</text>
  <text x="250" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-family="Segoe UI, sans-serif" fill="#0d366b" font-weight="600">candidates</text>

# Refit, then open the test rows

Cross-validation chose the one-feature model. Fit it on **all** the training
rows, then score it once on the test rows.

```{pyodide}
final = LinearRegression()
final.fit(train[A], train["vol_next"])

final_pred = final.predict(test[A])
print(np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(test["vol_next"], final_pred)))
```

::: {.muted .small}
The folds were only a way of estimating this number. With the choice made, the
model can use every training row.
:::

# What stays with you {.smaller}

::: {.recap-grid}
::: {.recap-item}
**Fitting a model**
`LinearRegression()`, `.fit(X, y)`, `.predict(X)`. Later models change only the first line.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**X is a table, y is a column**
`train[["vol_20d"]]` with two brackets, `train["vol_next"]` with one.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Always report a baseline**
Compare the model against the training average and against a simple rule that uses no model.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Training error always prefers more columns**
Adding a column can never worsen the fit, so training error cannot say whether the column helps.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Choosing uses up data**
Rows used to compare candidates can no longer give an honest score for the winner.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**One split is one measurement**
Moving the cut date can change the winner. Cross-validation averages over several cuts.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Read the folds, not only the mean**
A fold much worse than the others points to a period the model handles badly.
:::
::: {.recap-item}
**Folds must follow the calendar**
Use `TimeSeriesSplit` for a time series. `KFold` shuffles, and here it chose the worst of the three models.
:::
:::
